title: Noise-robust navigation from an adaptive run-and-tumble policy
abstract: How do organisms navigate when the signals guiding them are noisy? Variance adaptation, the rescaling of sensitivity to noise, is common in sensory systems, but its role in navigation is unexplored. We introduce a minimal active Brownian particle whose run-and-tumble policy follows from an optimality principle. Variance adaptation emerges as part of this policy. Adaptation keeps chemotactic drift finite as noise grows, while a non-adaptive particle's collapses exponentially. Adaptation also carries a cost, degrading performance in quiet environments and requiring a tuned adaptation sensitivity.
summary: This work develops a theoretical model for how organisms navigate using noisy sensory inputs, proposing that variance adaptation is key to robustness. By comparing adaptive and non-adaptive movement policies, the authors show that adaptation allows particles to maintain directed motion even when environmental noise is high. This provides a quantitative framework for understanding noise resilience in biological sensing and movement.
main_problem: The paper investigates how motile organisms maintain robust navigation when sensory signals are corrupted by noise, focusing on the role of variance adaptation in their movement policy.
main_result: Adaptive particles (AAP) significantly outperform constant-gain particles (CGAP) at high noise levels, demonstrating that variance adaptation is crucial for sustaining directed movement in noisy environments.
method: The policy is derived by maximizing a utility function subject to a relative entropy penalty, leading to the analysis of mean drift velocity using Fokker-Planck equation solutions and approximations.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a minimal active Brownian particle undergoing run-and-tumble motion, sensing a noisy signal $C(\mathbf{r},t) = S(\mathbf{r}) + \xi$. The particle's rotational diffusivity adapts based on the prediction error.
key_observables: Average response gain ($\langle G angle$) and mean drift velocity ($\langle v_d angle$) along the signal gradient.
important_parameters: Noise strength ($W$), adaptation sensitivity ($\alpha$), and the intrinsic diffusion constants ($D_t, D_r$).
main_assumptions: The analysis uses an approximation ($ eta\mu \ll \Theta$) for analytical tractability, and the adaptation mechanism is treated as costless.
figures_summary: Figures compare AAP and CGAP trajectories and plot average gain and drift velocity versus noise strength, showing AAP's superior performance at high noise.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the minimal active Brownian particle model, derives the optimal run-and-tumble policy incorporating variance adaptation, and then analyzes the resulting transport properties by comparing AAP and CGAP performance across varying noise levels.
why_interesting: While focused on biological motility, the underlying mathematical framework—optimality principles, noise filtering, and non-equilibrium steady states—shares conceptual links with open quantum systems where environmental noise dictates system dynamics and optimal control strategies.
